Sit with that. The benchmark used to grade AI on construction drawings is wrong. The general-purpose models are wrong. The human expert was off. And the person with multiple engineering degrees needed real time to get it right.

This is a single-family house. One sheet. Now scale it to a hospital: thousands of sheets, hundreds of revisions, symbols that mean different things on different disciplines' drawings.

This is why "just point Claude at your drawings" fails in construction. Reading a drawing isn't reading text. It's geometry, symbols, line weights, spatial relationships, and knowing that a swing arc means one thing and a closet opening without one means something else entirely.

Getting this right takes two things:

1. AI built for construction, not adapted to it. We trained our vision layer on millions of real jobsite documents: 400+ object types, 2M+ labels. Years of work, not a wrapper.

2. Teaching teams how to work with AI. Even great AI needs people who know when to trust it, when to check it, and how to fold it into their workflow. Tools alone don't make you faster. Tools plus training do. Which is what we do for EVERY SINGLE JOBSITE. 

We didn't come to construction from AI. We came to AI from construction.

📰 Trunk Tools in VentureBeat! This one gets into the technical foundation we've spent years getting right.

General-purpose AI wasn't built for construction. The data is too messy, the documents too dense, the workflows too high-stakes.

That's why we built something different:

 🧱 A three-layer architecture - data extraction, knowledge graph, autonomous agents trained on construction's actual data
 📄 Agents that reason across millions of pages, not just what fits in a context window
 ⏱ Document review cycles cut from 50–60 days down to 10–15

General-purpose LLMs are trained to be okay at everything. That makes them weak at anything requiring precision. And in construction, “probably right” isn't good enough - missed details cost real money and put real projects at risk.

We started with the hard problem: how do you make AI actually reliable for an industry built on documents, drawings, and complexity? The architecture we landed on is the answer.

Did you know that the median actual output for sanitary piping across commercial projects globally is 104 ft/week, while schedules assume 470 ft/week? 

This reveals a significant 78% gap, and it's not an isolated incident.

Buildots analysed planned versus actual weekly MEP output across HVAC, sanitary, domestic water, and electrical containment, and the findings show a consistent pattern: schedules assume 2x to 4x what crews actually deliver on a sustained basis. 

The issue lies not with the trades themselves, but with the assumptions embedded in the schedules. Until now, there has been no standardised method to determine what "normal" output looks like. Each project is planned from scratch, and every schedule is based on best-case scenarios.

Take a moment to review the numbers and consider how your projects measure up.

We’ve been doing some research lately at Buildots on performance indicators, specifically Production Attainment. While looking at the data, we found a strong correlation between hitting targets and weeks where activities had zero progress (when they should have).

It might sound trivial, but it isn't. Activities with ‘Zero-Progress Weeks’ don't just lose a week’s worth of progress. They also show much lower production attainment even months later.

We looked deeper at two common activities: drywall framing and mechanical ductwork. A consistent pattern showed up. In drywall, the drop in efficiency was sharp (30% drop for every Zero-Progress Week). In ductwork, the hit was smaller per week, but it compounded quickly.

We’re not suggesting this is a causation, it’s a correlation. But it shows up often enough that I now see a ‘Zero-Progress Week’ as a major warning light for workflow health.

I’m curious. Does this match what you see on your projects? Have you ever noticed anything like that?
Would love to learn from the discussion.

Across more than hundred of projects, sprinkler risers are the latest activity to meaningfully get going - 9.6 weeks later than the revised schedule says they should.
We analysed when each MEP activity reached 10% of its scope, completely filtering out the minor early work that can make an activity look like it's underway when it isn't.

Looking at riser activities specifically:
→ Sprinkler risers: 9.6 weeks late
→ Electrical riser containment: 4.7 weeks late
→ Riser mechanical ductwork: 1.4 weeks late

Medians, against the most recently revised schedule. Every riser activity in our dataset is behind plan.
Risers carry services between floors and feed commissioning. Delays to getting them going compress the commissioning window downstream, and that compression is hard to recover.

The consistency of the pattern is what stands out. Across projects, regions, and disciplines within the riser category, the direction is the same.

Curious whether this matches what people running fitouts are seeing on site right now.

How many doors do you see? 🚪 Look at this floor plan. Count the doors. I'll wait. Drop your count in the comments.

Here's what happened when we ran this exact question:

Fable said 8 (then hedged to "9-12").
ChatGPT's best model said 13.
The official AI benchmark this drawing comes from says the "ground truth" is 3. Three!
A construction subject matter expert said 8.
I have a PhD in civil engineering, 3 masters degrees and grew up on jobsites. It took me a solid chunk of time to find the answer... and it was different than any of the above.

Sit with that. The benchmark used to grade AI on construction drawings is wrong. The general-purpose models are wrong. The human expert was off. And the person with multiple engineering degrees needed real time to get it right.

This is a single-family house. One sheet. Now scale it to a hospital: thousands of sheets, hundreds of revisions, symbols that mean different things on different disciplines' drawings.

This is why "just point Claude at your drawings" fails in construction. Reading a drawing isn't reading text. It's geometry, symbols, line weights, spatial relationships, and knowing that a swing arc means one thing and a closet opening without one means something else entirely.

Getting this right takes two things:

1. AI built for construction, not adapted to it. We trained our vision layer on millions of real jobsite documents: 400+ object types, 2M+ labels. Years of work, not a wrapper.

2. Teaching teams how to work with AI. Even great AI needs people who know when to trust it, when to check it, and how to fold it into their workflow. Tools alone don't make you faster. Tools plus training do. Which is what we do for EVERY SINGLE JOBSITE. 

We didn't come to construction from AI. We came to AI from construction.

AI adoption does not stall because people are resistant to change.
It stalls because leadership alignment breaks down.

This came to mind as I listened to Eric Thomas on a recent episode of Digital Builder with guest Sarah Buchner from Trunk Tools. It moves past high-level AI talk and gets specific about why adoption actually stalls and what leaders can do about it.

A few takeaways that resonated:

▪️ AI adoption only works when the C-suite and the field are aligned. It cannot be bottom-up alone.
▪️ The biggest near-term gains are in information-heavy and coordination workflows, including documentation, scheduling, and search, where friction and rework quietly add risk.
▪️Tools fail when they add steps instead of removing pain. If the field does not see immediate value, adoption stops.
End-to-end automation matters because it reduces the need for behavior change, which is often the real blocker.

This reinforces that AI adoption is not a technology problem.

It is a leadership and value alignment problem, especially when data and workflows are not connected.

At its worst, AI becomes another layer teams are asked to adopt without clarity or confidence. 
At its best, it improves delivery certainty, reduces rework, and strengthens decision-making before issues reach the site

As a leader, where do you see the biggest gap today: tools, alignment, or decision-making clarity?

When we started ToolSense in 2017, it was born from a simple problem.

My co-founders Ross, Beni, and I were still at university when a friend at Hilti told us about expensive power tools disappearing from job sites. 

We built an IoT-based anti-theft solution - and it worked.

But once we connected to the equipment, we discovered something much bigger: every process around managing these assets was still completely manual. 

Paper-based, fragmented, inefficient.

That took us from anti-theft to building a horizontal asset and maintenance management platform - serving FM, construction, logistics, hospitality, and more.

Over the years, one thing became clear: facility management was where we saw the strongest growth, the deepest product-market fit, and the biggest opportunity.

Today, I'm excited to share that we are developing ToolSense towards becoming the leading FM Operations Platform - and that we've brought on GRO Capital to accelerate this journey.

Important: Our platform remains fully available and supported for all customers, especially construction.

We're doubling down on core capabilities - maintenance, IoT, parts & inventory, cost management, scheduling, and more. 

Our GTM is focusing on FM, but the platform will only get stronger for everyone who relies on it.

So - our customers actually showed us the way. 

What started as asset management expanded into quality audits, safety documentation, frontline task management, CAFM, and field service management.

Two massive shifts are reshaping FM: robotics and AI. 

Autonomous cleaning machines will become standard in commercial facilities. 

Managing robot fleets alongside traditional equipment requires a unified platform. 

AI is unlocking new possibilities - from predictive maintenance to intelligent workflow automation - but only when built on rich operational data.

These forces led to a clear decision: evolving ToolSense into a full FM Operations Platform.

We've been talking to GRO for over two years. 

They have a proven track record scaling vertical SaaS in asset-heavy industries - most notably building Trackunit into the leading IoT platform in construction, a journey with many parallels to ours.

With GRO on board, we're combining deep FM expertise with the playbook to scale internationally.

The FM industry still runs on paper, WhatsApp, and Excel. 

The tools haven't kept up with the job - or the possibilities AI enables. 

We're changing that.

ToolSense serves 200+ customers across 30+ countries - and we're just getting started. 

One platform for every asset, every workflow, every site.

No more paper. No more WhatsApp. No more Excel.

We're hiring across all sectors - please reach out to me directly if you are interested!

Andercore has raised $40m to build the AI-driven industrial trade and distribution platform.

Industrial trade is one of the largest and most critical systems in the global economy. Despite its scale, it remains operationally fragmented, slow, and heavily manual.

Coming from a fifth-generation trading and manufacturing heritage, I’ve seen firsthand how the core mechanics of trade – negotiation, pricing, quality assurance, logistics, and financing – have barely changed over time.
Over the past five years, we have built Andercore to operate this system differently - better.

Today, Andercore has secured $40m in equity and debt financing to further scale its AI-driven trade and distribution platform. The platform executes thousands of cross-border transactions each month across energy, infrastructure, and building materials, integrating pricing, quoting, quality assurance, logistics, and financing into a single operating system.

We built the platform by running real trade flows from day one. It was shaped by live transactions, supplier constraints, buyer behavior, and logistics execution – not by theoretical models, but with our established partners. 

Industrial buyers require speed, reliability, and predictable execution. Suppliers require market access, demand visibility, and disciplined counterparties. Our platform addresses these requirements as an operating system.

This financing round, led by Atomico (Andreas Helbig), Project A (Florian Heinemann), and Inven Capital (Petr Míkovec), alongside institutional financing from Commerzbank AG (Ralf-Dieter Jaschok) and KfW (Jochen Eichmann), is complemented by a group of experienced operators and founders, including FlixBus founders Daniel Krauss and Jochen Engert; home24 SE Founder Philipp Kreibohm, and former Klöckner CEO Gisbert Ruehl.

11 beavers did something in Scotland that scientists’ computers say is impossible.

They were brought in to help a dying river. Only modest changes were expected…

But instead, something incredible happened:

🌧️ Water retention increased to 60%
🌊 Flood peaks were cut in half
🦌 Biodiversity started spreading in areas that were deemed as irrecoverable.
🐟 Salmon returned
💐 Wildflower meadows were restored
🐞 Dragonflies and frogs and wetland creatures came back

It went from a dry, lifeless crack to a spongy vibrant wetland

Over 100 dams now step down the Knapdale valleys: each one catching, storing, and gradually releasing water.

A self-maintaining flood defense system built from mud and sticks that outperformed decades of concrete engineering.

Beavers are the best ecologists and engineers we could ever imagine.

The University of Stirling hydrologist put it simply:

"Our computer models couldn't reproduce what actually happened."

But the results came with trade-offs:

Flooded fields, complex compensation systems, and growing tension between ecological restoration and agricultural livelihoods

It forced Scotland to confront a harder question:

Not whether nature can outperform engineered solutions, but how far society is willing to let it.

This is the story of how a handful of animals rewrote centuries of river management, and why restoring nature is never as simple as letting it back in.

When will we start implementing more systems designed from nature’s wisdom and less from our limited imagination?

content:
A few takeaways from a great article by Marty Cagan for PMs:

🧠 Build to learn = build for the purpose of discovering what to build.
💵 Build to earn = ship the thing that you are going to sell.

Very helpful framing, and it's easier said than done when you're one product team among many.

Here are a few things that I keep in mind when I build to learn right now:

1️⃣ "I don't own that area of the product" is not a valid excuse. If my job is to solve a problem, my solution space is the entire product. PMs who only understand their slice, propose solutions that are artificially constrained.

2️⃣ It's easy to build a prototype that teaches you nothing. My job is to build one that gives me real signal about what to build. Especially in B2B, you have to think upfront about what "working" looks, which customers you're putting it in front of, and what you're measuring. Plan the delivery infrastructure upfront: feature flags, segments, clean rollback (shoutout LaunchDarkly). You need to ship prototypes to a subset, watch what happens, and pull it back without drama.

3️⃣ In a multi-team org, people adopt the product model at different speeds, and that can slow you down if you are the first one moving faster. A live-data prototype looks identical to a feature launch from the outside: code shipped to real users. But you didn't take it through product review, design didn't audit it for pixel-perfection, and you didn't socialize a tech plan with adjacent eng teams. If you wait until you're mid-experiment to explain why that's okay, you'll get slow-walked in the name of "process." Put the work in now. Find a fast approach to align on what a live-data prototype is and isn't. You'll remove roadblocks and learn faster when the coast is clear.

content:
I joined Higharc last month to help build AI for homebuilding. In drafting & architecture, the theoretical reach of AI looks enormous, almost as large as coding, but observed usage has lagged. A month into working with the Higharc Labs team (our mission: deliver frontier AI research that makes housing faster to build and more affordable), I'm starting to understand why.

Two reasons stand out:

1. Most architectural data is pure geometry. Points, lines, and planes in 3D space. A single home design can run you ~6 GB and I'd bet that if you opened the raw file, you couldn't guess it's a house. There are slick demos of models driving CAD tools, but they're pushing an expensive LLM uphill on a representation that fights back. Higharc encodes homes differently: structured, semantic data measured in ~10 MB. That lets us train models on data the frontier labs simply don't have. Check out the cool video of something we are working on. When we do reach for a frontier LLM, an older generation often does the job, because our data is easier to reason over.

2. There is no margin for error. Production homebuilders run on high-single-digit net margins (~6–9%). When an estimator writes a bill of materials for an entire house, the error allowance is measured in inches. The bet at Higharc is that with the right data, models, and evaluations in place, AI can finally start to help with that.

The thing that makes me bullish is the people. Higharc's implementation team is full of folks who designed and architected homes in a past life, and the company has attracted seemingly every architect who later became an engineer or AI researcher. With that expertise embedded directly in the people building the technology, the iteration loop is incredibly tight.

Grateful to be on this team, and excited for the challenges ahead. Thanks to Michael Bergin, Marc Minor, and Caspar Y. for bringing me on to work on a hard, important problem.

content:
Ten years ago, AlphaGo played Move 37 against Lee Sedol. A move so unexpected that some thought it was a mistake.

It wasn’t intuition alone that produced that move. AlphaGo could search possible futures, test its instincts and reason about what would happen next.

In a new piece for MIT Technology Review, I argue that today’s most advanced AI systems still lack that kind of reasoning.

LLMs have become remarkably capable, and giving them more time to “think” has delivered real gains. But generating longer chains of thought is not the same as having a separate reasoning process that can track what is known, what remains uncertain, what evidence supports a conclusion and whether genuine progress has been made.

This is why I recently left Google DeepMind. I believe we need a fresh approach to machine reasoning. One that takes some of the architectural lessons from AlphaGo and applies them to much more open-ended problems.

If AI is going to produce genuinely novel and trustworthy insights in areas like science, medicine and engineering, its conclusions need to arise from an auditable process of evidence, inference and belief revision.

Many thanks to Rachel Courtland and the MIT Technology Review team for commissioning. You can find the link to the full piece in the comments.

content:
I joined Higharc last month to help build AI for homebuilding. In drafting & architecture, the theoretical reach of AI looks enormous, almost as large as coding, but observed usage has lagged. A month into working with the Higharc Labs team (our mission: deliver frontier AI research that makes housing faster to build and more affordable), I'm starting to understand why.

Two reasons stand out:

1. Most architectural data is pure geometry. Points, lines, and planes in 3D space. A single home design can run you ~6 GB and I'd bet that if you opened the raw file, you couldn't guess it's a house. There are slick demos of models driving CAD tools, but they're pushing an expensive LLM uphill on a representation that fights back. Higharc encodes homes differently: structured, semantic data measured in ~10 MB. That lets us train models on data the frontier labs simply don't have. Check out the cool video of something we are working on. When we do reach for a frontier LLM, an older generation often does the job, because our data is easier to reason over.

2. There is no margin for error. Production homebuilders run on high-single-digit net margins (~6–9%). When an estimator writes a bill of materials for an entire house, the error allowance is measured in inches. The bet at Higharc is that with the right data, models, and evaluations in place, AI can finally start to help with that.

The thing that makes me bullish is the people. Higharc's implementation team is full of folks who designed and architected homes in a past life, and the company has attracted seemingly every architect who later became an engineer or AI researcher. With that expertise embedded directly in the people building the technology, the iteration loop is incredibly tight.

Grateful to be on this team, and excited for the challenges ahead. Thanks to Michael Bergin, Marc Minor, and Caspar Y. for bringing me on to work on a hard, important problem.

Supabase → Grasshopper → Speckle
Grasshopper is incredibly powerful at processing data, but it isn’t designed to store it. 

Yet many parametric workflows rely on structured data: 
• material data
• embodied carbon values • cost information 
• element properties 
• design run results 

And storing this locally in scripts or spreadsheets quickly becomes messy. 

Instead, these datasets can live in a central database. 
In this example I connected Grasshopper to Supabase. 

Supabase is essentially a PostgreSQL database with a clean UI and a simple REST API. Which means we can query it directly from Grasshopper. In the demo: 
• material data is stored in the database 
• Grasshopper queries that data in real time 
• the parametric wall assembly updates automatically 

Then using Speckle Intelligence, those material properties are tracked all the way into the output BIM model. This turns parametric models into data-driven systems, not just geometry generators. 

This setup gives all the scaling benefits of a proper relational database. The leverage is in the long-term robustness of this setup. You can build or connect with apps and dashboards and manage users and their access policies.

The 400 million tokens aren't measuring the building. They're measuring the serialization.

Martyn asks the right question below: what should the machine receive instead? A textual IFC export is already a derivative - the model's database flattened into text, and the syntax is most of the tokens. The source, one step upstream, is a **database**.

So give the machine the database. Properties as rows, relationships as edges, geometry parked where a language model never needs to read it. "Find the door, its host wall, fire rating and sheet reference" becomes a join that runs in milliseconds and returns a couple of kilobytes: the schema, the question, the answer. Not hypothetical: at Speckle we run SQL over 26-million-element models in a browser tab.

The context window is working memory, not storage. The models are ready. Our industry just needs to stop handing them documents and start handing them databases.

Am researching current AI memory limitations vs BIM models. I asked Claude; How long before a 1.5GB BIM model fits in an AI context window?

It did the arithmetic. The answer was less encouraging than I expected.
A 1.5GB textual IFC export represents roughly 300–500 million tokens, depending on the file and tokenizer. The largest generally available production context windows are around 1–2 million tokens. The gap is therefore still hundreds of times.
Context windows grew astonishingly quickly—from about 2,000 tokens in 2020 to one or two million in 2024. Since then, the public frontier has largely plateaued. The problem is no longer simply whether a larger window can be demonstrated. It is whether it can be served economically, with acceptable latency and reliable recall.
At current advertised API rates, sending 400 million input tokens would theoretically cost hundreds or thousands of dollars per query, if any production model could accept the request. Caching could reduce repeated costs, but a live BIM model changes continuously, and huge-context inference would remain an extraordinarily inefficient way to answer a small question.
To find one door, its host wall, fire rating and sheet reference, an agent does not need 400 million tokens. It needs a structured query, a handful of connected objects and enough context to reason about the result.
That is a difference of several orders of magnitude—and it grows as projects get larger.
You don’t read the entire library to answer a question. You use the catalogue.
The context window was never the database. The model was never meant to be the prompt.
So what should the machine receive instead?

Implementation is the difference between adoption and abandonment.

Having spent many years in the field, I've seen it happen more times than I can count. A company invests in a new platform with high expectations, but within a few months they're back to marking up PDFs, manually matching photos to deficiencies, chasing updates through email, and tracking corrective actions in spreadsheets. They end up spending more time managing inspections than performing them and conclude the software just wasn't a good fit.

More often than not, that wasn't the real issue.

Successful implementation isn't just about onboarding and training. It's about understanding your workflows, configuring the platform around them, and having a Customer Success team that stays engaged long after go live.
At PlanRadar, we work alongside our customers from day one to tailor the platform to their processes, not force their processes to fit the platform. That partnership continues well beyond implementation, helping ensure long term adoption and lasting value.

When evaluating software, don't just ask for a demo.

Ask what implementation looks like.

Ask who will support you after the contract is signed.

Those answers will often tell you more than the feature list ever could.

Last night I presented alongside Martin Fischer. One question kept surfacing: what if we've been trying to fix the wrong thing all along? 

For those who don't know him, he's affectionately known as the founding father of #VDC. Stanford, CIFE, decades of shaping how this industry thinks about digital delivery. The kind of person whose work follows you through a #PhD. In fact, I cited him quite a bit in mine, so sharing a stage with him meant a lot to me. 

His diagnosis has always been sharp. #BIM is a means to an end, not the end. The industry confused the tool for the outcome. And for the last thirty years, our answer has been to build rigorous management frameworks around BIM to bridge the gap between what the model contains and what people actually need to know (VDC, integrated delivery, collaborative planning). But the reality is that the industry hasn't been able to make those processes stick at scale. 

I believe that's not a failure of those processes, it's evidence that the foundation was wrong. Since starting Speckle, I've landed on a different approach. I think the gap is architectural, not organisational. Communication is inferential. Meaning is constructed by the receiver, not transmitted by the sender. The data layer itself has to do that work, rather than the process wrapped around it. 

That belief is what Speckle is built on. What made last night interesting for me is that the field's best thinkers have been circling this problem for thirty years. The question isn't whether the industry needs to change. It's whether we continue trying to fix the process, or if we take a step back and tackle fixing the foundation. Grateful to have been in the room, thanks Bricks & Bytes for hosting.

Also big shoutout to Owen, Matt, Alain, David, Anthony, Marzia, Andrew (for hosting us at Introba!) and all the other attendees for the post-presentation fun chats, gossip and good old human interaction!

A client asks you to show, with actual data benchmarks, how your last 20 projects informed the one you're pitching them now. Could you do it?

Most firms can't.

The evidence exists. That much we know. But can you get to it? 

Most firms can't.

Knowledge that's sitting inside project folders nobody opens after handover, archived in formats nobody can query, sitting in software versions no longer in production... Is it really knowledge? Does it serve its purpose?

Listen to this:

We know that one global design studio with 500+ people wanted to build portfolio intelligence. They started with 744 completed projects.
They ended up with 38 that they could actually analyze.

95% of their most valuable knowledge - inaccessible.
They also found 299 different names for what was essentially a "meeting room."
299 different names...

This is the feedback loop AEC never built. Every project starts from scratch. Benchmarks get assembled manually. "Intuition" takes the place of actual evidence. Decades of built work sit in folders generating 0 return.

So here's what we think is a no-brainer fact: firms knocking it out of the park in the next decades will be the ones asking the right questions:

- What space mix performs best for law firms in high-rise towers?
- What do our most satisfied healthcare clients have in common?
- Which structural approaches deliver the best constructibility at this scale?

And today, this problem is truly breathing down our collective necks because, let's all say it together: AI.
AI doesn't improve our messy projects. It scales our evidence. If we don't have evidence, we just get faster guesses, and AEC can't risk this.

That's not a futuristic scenario. Portfolio intelligence compounds. The firm that starts today will have a multi-year advantage that's nearly impossible to replicate quickly. 

Are you capturing data today in a way that will be queryable in five years?
